faq.q: Can gout present with a normal uric acid level?

faq.a: If the patient has fever, leukocytosis, or a history of skin infection, treat as septic until proven otherwise.
faq.q: When should I suspect septic arthritis instead of gout?

faq.a: Colchicine can accumulate; use reduced dose or choose steroids if renal function is poor.

exam: A 48‑year‑old farmer presents with 2‑day sudden pain in the right first MTP joint, no fever. What is your next diagnostic step and why? — Perform joint aspiration to look for urate crystals; if unavailable, start NSAID therapy and arrange follow‑up.

A patient with known gout develops fever and worsening swelling of the first MTP joint. How does this change your management? — Treat as possible septic arthritis: obtain aspirate, start empiric IV antibiotics, and consider surgical drainage.
Explain why serum uric acid alone cannot rule out gout in an acute attack. — Levels may be normal during attacks; crystal analysis is definitive.

What are the key features that differentiate septic arthritis from gout clinically? — Fever, systemic toxicity, leukocytosis, purulent aspirate versus rapid onset pain with erythema but no systemic signs.

List three lifestyle measures that reduce future gout attacks and the physiological rationale. — Reduce purine intake (less uric acid production), increase water intake (enhances renal excretion), limit alcohol (decreases uric acid clearance).

A patient cannot take NSAIDs due to renal disease. Which alternative acute gout treatment is preferred and why? — Colchicine is preferred because it does not affect renal prostaglandins; steroids are second line if colchicine contraindicated.
Describe the radiographic changes seen in chronic gout of the first MTP joint. — Erosions with overhanging edges and soft‑tissue tophi; may be absent early.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt immediate surgical referral for the first MTP joint? — Rapidly enlarging, fluctuant swelling with skin breakdown suggesting septic arthritis or osteomyelitis.

ai.summary: The first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint is the most common site of acute gout (podagra) and can also be affected by infection, trauma, and osteoarthritis. Recognising the pattern of pain, swelling and systemic clues guides urgent and long‑term management, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Red, hot, swollen joint with severe pain on passive dorsiflexion
History of rapid onset (hours) favors crystal arthritis or septic arthritis
sections.p: The first MTP joint is the articulation between the first metatarsal head and the proximal phalanx of the hallux. Acute inflammation is diagnosed clinically and confirmed by joint aspiration when possible.

Severe: fever, systemic toxicity, or suspected infection

sections.p: Patients describe sudden, excruciating pain in the big toe, often after a heavy meal or alcohol intake. The joint becomes erythematous, warm, and swollen; the patient may be unable to bear weight.

Uric acid: supportive, not definitive

b: Gout: NSAID (e.g., ibuprofen) if no renal contraindication; colchicine if NSAID contraindicated; steroids (oral or intra‑articular) for refractory cases
Septic arthritis: Empiric IV ceftriaxone plus gentamicin (adjust for local resistance); surgical drainage if pus present
Trauma: Immobilisation, analgesia, and referral for fracture if suspected
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then control pain and inflammation. Choose drugs that are available and safe in low‑resource settings.

Consider allopurinol or febuxostat when chronic hyperuricaemia persists
sections.p: Arrange review within 3‑5 days to assess response. Long‑term gout prevention includes lifestyle change and urate‑lowering therapy when available.
